reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Anal intraepithelial neoplasia is a human papillomavirus-driven premalignant squamous dysplasia of the anal canal and margin, the precursor of anal squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded as low-grade or high-grade dysplasia; contemporary terminology aligns with the two-tier low-grade and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion system

High-risk HPV (especially type 16) is the principal driver; major risk groups include people living with HIV, men who have sex with men, immunosuppressed transplant recipients, and those with prior HPV-related anogenital neoplasia
It is frequently asymptomatic and detected incidentally, or presents with pruritus, discomfort, bleeding, discharge, or a visible lesion
Diagnosis relies on high-resolution anoscopy with targeted biopsy, aided by acetic acid and Lugol iodine staining to identify dysplastic areas
High-grade disease carries a risk of progression to invasive carcinoma, which is heightened in immunosuppressed patients, so surveillance is central
Management is individualised and ranges from surveillance to topical therapies, ablation, and targeted excision, balancing recurrence and multifocality against the morbidity of wide excision
Any suspicion of invasion mandates biopsy and staging, as invasive anal cancer is managed quite differently, typically with chemoradiotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, principally type 16, is the central driver of anal intraepithelial neoplasia. Viral oncoproteins inactivate host tumour-suppressor pathways (notably p53 and retinoblastoma protein function), driving unregulated proliferation of squamous epithelium of the anal transformation zone and margin. Dysplastic cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes, producing progressive loss of maturation and architectural disorder that defines low-grade and then high-grade neoplasia. Immunosuppression, as in HIV infection or transplantation, impairs viral clearance and immune surveillance, favouring persistence, multifocality, and progression. High-grade lesions may, over time, breach the basement membrane to become invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Perianal Bowen disease and extramammary Paget disease
Anal skin tags or benign fibroepithelial lesions
Chronic anal dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus or eczema
Haemorrhoids or fissure as a cause of bleeding
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution anoscopy with acetic acid and Lugol iodine and targeted biopsy
Histopathological grading of biopsies to confirm and stage dysplasia
HPV testing and anal cytology where used in screening pathways
HIV testing and assessment of immune status
Examination under anaesthesia and mapping biopsies for extensive disease
Staging imaging (MRI and nodal assessment) if invasion is suspected
redFlags: An indurated, ulcerated, or bleeding mass suggesting invasive carcinoma
Rapid change or progression of a known lesion
High-grade dysplasia in an immunosuppressed patient
A non-healing anal ulcer or fissure in an at-risk individual
reference.prognosis: Low-grade lesions frequently regress and rarely progress, whereas high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia carries a real, if variable, risk of progression to invasive cancer, greatest in immunosuppressed patients; recurrence after treatment is common, so long-term surveillance is required and early detection of invasion is key to outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming a visible anal lesion is a simple wart or tag and omitting biopsy
Failing to recognise and stage occult invasive carcinoma within apparent dysplasia
Overlooking screening in high-risk groups such as people living with HIV
Performing wide excision that risks stenosis when multifocal disease will recur regardless
Neglecting long-term surveillance after treatment of high-grade disease
